part_title: Operational AI Runbooks, Privacy, Governance and Bedrock Evaluation Lab

scenes.title: Operational runbook for model errors and throttles
scenes.narration: This slide is a practical decision flow for model-invocation failures. First classify the response. A client error, such as an invalid parameter or access denial, often requires fixing the request, supported model or permissions rather than repeated retries. A temporary five-hundred-level service failure may be retryable with bounded exponential backoff and jitter. Throttling means request or token limits are being exceeded, so reduce concurrency, batch where appropriate, review quotas and add controlled retry behavior. The middle panels show the evidence to examine: requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent invocations, IAM permissions and model availability in the selected Region. After applying a targeted fix, confirm that errors decline, latency remains acceptable and the complete user workflow works. Finally, add alerts and capacity reviews to prevent recurrence. One important safety detail: a retry after a timeout can create duplicate business effects if the workflow is not idempotent. This is why model calls and surrounding tool actions require different recovery decisions. Classify first, remediate specifically, then verify with metrics and representative requests.

scenes.title: Observability Data Privacy Review
scenes.narration: This diagram is a privacy checklist for logs, metrics, traces and operational events. Follow the columns: inventory the fields the application records, detect sensitive information, minimise or redact it, choose retention periods, restrict access, encrypt storage and transport, and audit usage. The example table includes personal identifiers, email addresses, IP information and payment data, with redacted versions to illustrate what should reach telemetry. Notice the retention column. High-sensitivity records may require a shorter retention window than aggregated performance metrics, but the correct duration depends on policy and legal obligations. The access-control column emphasises least privilege and periodic review, while encryption and key management protect the stored records. Audit trails help establish who changed logging configuration or accessed sensitive operational data. Redaction must happen before telemetry is exported to other systems, not just when someone opens a dashboard. For a GenAI assistant, raw prompts, retrieved documents and responses can contain confidential content. Treat observability as a designed data-processing pipeline with its own security controls.

scenes.title: The Integrated Governance Loop
scenes.narration: This slide ties the entire module into a repeated operational cycle. Begin with Evaluate: run quality and safety tests, inspect difficult cases, and capture evidence that a model or prompt meets its release threshold. Next, Deploy carefully with guardrails, approvals and a staged rollout. Observe real traffic using latency, cost, quality signals and user feedback. Detect unusual behavior and incidents. Investigate with traces, logs, retrieved evidence and reproducible examples to find the root cause. Finally, Improve the prompt, retrieval pipeline, model or safeguards, then feed the corrected case back into evaluation. Look at the ownership and evidence boxes around the loop. Model evaluation, AI engineering, platform operations, incident response and governance teams have distinct responsibilities. Evaluation reports, deployment records, dashboards and post-incident findings create an audit trail. This is not a linear checklist you finish once. New datasets, user behavior and model updates can create new problems, so the cycle continues throughout the application's life. The goal is safe, measurable improvement rather than frequent changes without evidence.

scenes.title: Lab overview: Evaluate a Bedrock generative AI endpoint before release
scenes.narration: The lab overview shows a complete evaluation-to-monitoring exercise. Start with an S3 prompt dataset containing representative tasks and expected behaviors. Configure a Bedrock evaluation job for the model under review, selecting the task and relevant metrics. The next panel represents model responses and evaluation results, including answer relevancy, groundedness, summarisation quality and toxicity. These figures are illustrative and should not be treated as real model benchmarks. The final CloudWatch area will be used to watch quality signals as the application operates. Notice the deliberately incomplete starting state at the bottom: the model endpoint exists, but the evaluation baseline and CloudWatch alarms have not been configured. That is what the learner is expected to fix. The goals are to run the evaluation, inspect both summary scores and individual examples, preserve a baseline and configure useful monitoring. For the actual lab, verify the available Bedrock model, evaluation job permissions, S3 location and appropriate metrics in the current console. Evaluation evidence matters only if it can be reproduced and tied to the specific model and prompt configuration.

scenes.title: Console walkthrough: prepare an evaluation dataset
scenes.narration: This final slide is a console walkthrough for preparing the dataset needed by the Bedrock evaluation job. Follow the numbered screenshots. First, open Amazon S3 and create a private bucket in the intended Region; choose a globally unique bucket name and keep Block Public Access enabled. Next, upload the JSONL evaluation objects. The example includes question-answer, safety and reasoning datasets. Finally, open one object and inspect its content rather than assuming the upload succeeded. JSONL means one valid JSON object on each line. In this sample, a record contains a prompt, a reference answer and a category label. The preview includes questions about S3 storage, dataset versioning and security. Before proceeding, check that each record parses correctly, its expected-answer field uses the schema required by your evaluation configuration, and no secrets or personal information were included. Keep dataset file names versioned so future model comparisons use the same test inputs. The slide prepares the evaluation data; creating the bucket alone does not start a Bedrock evaluation. The next lab action would be to configure the evaluation job to read this approved S3 dataset.
